entry.title: Jimmy Yihang Zhong: Experimental S-sider
entry.content:
As an experimental s-sider, my research focuses on experimental linguistics (both acquisition and processing), grounded in theories of syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and their interfaces (s-side). Ontologically, I appreciate linguistic limits (i.e. how much specific subsystems can vary across languages) and predictors (i.e. what features may co-occur cross-linguistically). Epistemologically, I believe that linguistics is ultimately a part of cognitive science. Hence, I investigate how the language-specific biological faculty operates during language comprehension and production, and how it integrates into the broader context of the mind and brain (i.e. general cognitive faculty). Methodologically, I employ various behavioral and neural methods in experimental science to explore the interaction between linguistic theory and cognitive architecture.

Inspired by the natural sciences, my research in experimental linguistics follows a theory-driven, hypothetico-deductive logic, pursuing falsifiability and statistical validation. Its defining characteristic lies in its focus on implicit mental representations, which must be measured indirectly through experimental tasks, with variable operationalization relying on rigorous grammatical control. The measurement tools in my work are highly theory-laden; experimental design is deeply coupled with theoretical structural analysis, forming a philosophical paradigm of reciprocal validation between theory and experimentation.

A subsidiary thread that runs consistently through my work is the philosophy of language science, which interrogates the epistemological and ontological foundations of linguistic inquiry. For instance, I examine the legitimacy of Galilean idealization in formal linguistics, the falsifiability and resilience of theoretical frameworks, the modal distinction between necessary truth and accidental empirical generalization, and the disciplinary identity of linguistics within the broader architecture of cognitive science. I critically engage with tensions between rationalist and empiricist methodologies, the theoretical challenge posed by large language models, and the criteria that distinguish epistemically grounded research from merely nominal interdisciplinarity. This philosophical strand does not stand apart from my experimental program but rather underpins it. I aim to clarify what counts as genuine explanation, how theoretical constructs interface with experimental evidence, and how linguistics can maintain its disciplinary integrity while contributing meaningfully to the science of the mind.

entry.title: Linguistics Club For High School Students
entry.content:
Reflecting upon my experience running a linguistics club for high school students, I often look back fondly on the rewarding time I spent leading the club at a top international department, a stark contrast to my first attempt at an ordinary public school where student turnout was disappointingly low. Back then, I made three key clarifications to help students understand linguistics: it has nothing to do with learning languages themselves; it is not merely a branch of the humanities and social sciences; and while laypeople see language as a dish to be tasted and enjoyed with proper etiquette, linguists study its underlying “atoms and molecules”, the core principles that make language function.

Unlike many other high school linguistics clubs in China, which focus on popular science topics like the differences in how various languages distinguish colors, how Siri understands human speech, or why Chinese is considered difficult to learn, my background in professional linguistics drove me to set a different goal: to introduce undergraduate and master’s level professional linguistics, rather than scattered, unstructured trivia. When I joined the international department, I was delighted to discover that some students in the club even planned to pursue linguistics as their major in college.

In the precious span of less than two months, I led engaging workshops: in phonetics, I taught students the acoustic principles of natural linguistics, the International Phonetic Alphabet applicable to all human languages, and used Praat software to help them visualize their own voices by analyzing pitch, intensity, and duration. In syntax, I introduced basic generative theories, including X-bar theory and syntactic movement. They challenged these high-achieving students, especially when faced with complex hierarchical structures. A memorable moment was tackling the ambiguous phrase “the dog that bit the hunter”, which stumped both the students and me until I researched academic resources for a comprehensive solution. I also delivered an open class on generative syntax diagramming with AI assistance, which drew a large audience and received enthusiastic feedback, filling me with a strong sense of accomplishment.

This experience remains a cherished part of my journey, a testament to the curiosity and potential of young minds, and a reminder of the value of introducing rigorous academic linguistics to students eager to explore beyond the surface of language.

entry.title: Life
entry.content:
I'm a tennis player.

I started my training when I was 12. From 14-17, I participated more than 100 amateur tournament matches and won many trophies. After becoming a grown-up, I play less but still enjoy competition.

I'm a content creator.

Beyond my academic research, I also share my journey and insights on RedNote, a popular social media platform, where I build a community around linguistics, cognitive science, and the realities of academic life. As a content creator, my primary focus is making the often niche and technical world of linguistics more accessible to students, enthusiasts, and curious minds. I share practical study tips, reflections on research challenges, and discussions on core linguistic theories, all while maintaining the depth and rigor that define my work.

These posts aim to demystify academic research, offering a window into the life of a young linguist navigating the complexities of cross-disciplinary inquiry, peer review, and the evolving landscape of cognitive science. While linguistics forms the backbone of my content, I also open up about other aspects of my life and interests, creating a more well-rounded portrait beyond the lab.

My goal is to connect with a diverse audience, both within and outside the academic sphere, fostering conversations about language, cognition, and the pursuit of knowledge. For international visitors to my website, this space offers a glimpse into how I bridge my professional work with broader public engagement, using social media to share knowledge, spark curiosity, and build a supportive community around the fields I am passionate about.

entry.title: Frequently Asked Questions
entry.content:
Quick Navigation

  • What do you study and what don’t you study?
  • What journals and scholars interest you most?
  • How do you think of the current status of generative linguistics in relation to science?
  • How to become a linguist? What qualities are needed?
  • What are your most influential social media posts about linguistics?
  • What is your academic aspiration in a long run?
  • May I collaborate with you?
  • How may I contact you?

Q: What do you study and what don’t you study?

A: My core inquiry lies in experimental linguistics conceived in a broad sense, covering formal linguistic foundations, first and second language acquisition, developmental patterns from childhood to adulthood, and real‑time sentence comprehension and production across populations. Methodologically, I integrate behavioral methods (including but definitely not limited to acceptability judgment, self‑paced reading, elicited production) and neural imaging methods (e.g. EEG, fMRI) to probe mental representations and cognitive mechanisms, while remaining theoretically anchored in syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and their interfaces. Despite this wide scope, my research is consistently guided by a hypothetico‑deductive, falsifiability‑oriented scientific logic, with tightly coupled theoretical analysis and experimental design that prioritizes precise structural control and epistemic rigor. This broad‑based, multi‑method, multi‑population framework serves a unified agenda: to uncover the computational design, constraints, and developmental trajectory of the language faculty as part of human cognitive architecture.

I do not pursue research that drifts from linguistic phenomena, structural reality, or any ontological foundation of language. Accordingly, I stand against some versions of “applied linguistics” that abandon the study of language structure and internal mechanisms, instead reducing inquiry to external social, educational, or policy‑oriented problem‑solving WITHOUT epistemic grounding in linguistic theory. I also do not engage in purely atheoretical, data‑driven description, surface‑level interdisciplinarity, or disciplinary “problem‑feeding” that erodes the core identity and explanatory coherence of linguistics. I do not treat language as a neutral tool to investigate general cognition alone, nor do I reduce linguistic inquiry to engineering performance or social intervention without commitment to structural explanation. In short, while rejecting any “applied” agenda that loses touch with the empirical and theoretical foundations of language as its central object, my work embodies a methodologically applied, interdisciplinary orientation that translates formal theories and structural insights into testable experiments and empirically grounded cognitive models.

Q: What journals and scholars interest you most?

A: I especially enjoy reading Applied Psycholinguistics, Language Acquisition, Language, and Cognitive Science. They cover the processing field, the acquisition field, the general linguistics field, and the broad spectrum of cognitive science. I hope to contribute my works to these excellent journals.

I admire Jon Sprouse, an experimental linguist. His goal is to map out the hypothesis space of possible combinatorial systems in natural languages that could be implemented in the brain (at some level of abstraction). He is so knowledgeable about various behavioral and neuro research methods and shows methodological transparency on his website!

Q: How do you think of the current status of generative linguistics in relation to science?

A: I argue that generative linguistics can and should retain its theoretical core by adopting a clear domain of Galilean idealization, explicit interface parameters that link the abstract system to performance factors, and a standard of constrained consistency across experiments. This framework justifies idealization as a legitimate scientific strategy, while distinguishing the core computational system from extra-domain cognitive systems such as memory, attention, and inhibitory control. It does not seek isomorphism between formal structures and observable behavior, but requires predictable, coherent patterns across multiple measures.

Meanwhile, I fully understand another influential critique: if generative linguistics claims to study the biological foundation of language, it must abide by the empirical standards of natural and cognitive sciences; if it chooses to remain a pure formal discipline, it should avoid linking itself to biological or psychological mechanisms. From this perspective, any position between the two risks becoming inconsistent and unaccountable, as it can't satisfy the standards of either formal inquiry or empirical science. This view insists that the field must choose a clear identity rather than remaining in an ambiguous middle ground.

I continue to reflect deeply on this tension. Even as I advocate for integrating formal idealization and empirical constraint, many critical questions remain open: how many interface parameters are sufficient to maintain theoretical coherence? How stringent should cross-disciplinary evidence be in evaluating formal models? To what extent should a priori formal reasoning yield to behavioral and neural data? These issues occupy a complex, gray area with no straightforward answers, and I remain committed to exploring them rigorously.

Q: How to become a linguist? What qualities are needed?

A: To become a linguist, you first need a deep, unshakable curiosity about language as a window into the human mind and/or social reality (depending upon your philosophical stance), not just how we speak, but why we speak the way we do. This requires grounding yourself in the core of linguistic theory: phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and their interfaces, to build a precise understanding of natural languages. Equally critical is a commitment to methodological rigor, whether through formal analysis, experimental design, or philosophical inquiry, as the best work bridges theoretical speculation with empirical evidence.

Qualitatively, the most essential trait is intellectual resilience. As my own journey shows, academic paths are rarely linear. Rejections, funding shifts, and disciplinary biases are inevitable, but they refine your focus rather than define your worth. You must also cultivate philosophical clarity: understanding not just how to answer questions, but why they matter, and how to organize your thoughts to broader audiences. Finally, you need the courage to stay true to your intellectual identity, balancing interdisciplinary curiosity with the integrity of your core discipline.

Q: What are your most influential social media posts about linguistics?

A: I disseminate my views on linguistics and scientific research on RedNote, a social media platform. Here are some most influential posts (translated in English)👇
⭐Review of SSCI linguistics journals
⭐A video takes you through the development of modern linguistics over the past century
⭐Where is the future path for us who study linguistics?
⭐The misnomer applied linguistics is on the decline: whose fault is it
⭐The survival predicament of niche disciplines and what constitutes truly important research
⭐I failed at all 8 universities in my PhD linguistics applications. Where exactly did I lose?

Q: What is your academic aspiration in a long run?

A: Now I just want to be admitted by a PhD program. In the longer term, I plan to establish a journal titled Experimental Syntax/Semantics/Pragmatics and serve as its editor-in-chief. The journal will feature only high-quality studies with original theoretical contributions and rigorous cross-verification between linguistic theories and experimental findings. I aim to secure sponsorship to make it fully open-access, allowing free access for readers and free publication for authors. With sufficient financial support in the future, I also hope to build a linguistics museum to popularize this academic field.

Q: May I collaborate with you?

A: I welcome collaborators who share a theory-driven, hypothesis-testing mindset and a commitment to theoretical clarity, methodological rigor, and replicable empirical work. Ideal partners value linguistic reasoning, understand syntax-semantics-pragmatics representations, and respect the logic of falsifiability, statistical validation, and theory-experiment mutual constraint. They communicate transparently, meet deadlines reliably, take ownership of their role, and aim for cumulative, interpretable findings.

We may not be a nice fit if your work is purely descriptive, seeks so-called application WITHOUT epistemic grounding in linguistic theory, or has little interest in hypothesis testing about linguistic theory and cognitive mechanisms. This includes researchers focusing only on language teaching, classroom pedagogy, translation practices, sociolinguistic surveys, critical discourse analysis, computational modeling without cognitive interpretability, or large‑scale corpus description unconstrained by linguistic theory. Collaboration is also challenging if you prioritize social issues or qualitative interpretation over falsifiable predictions and statistical validation.

Q: How may I contact you?

A: You may contact me via email: yihang.zhong@link.cuhk.edu.hk.

entry.title: How I View Linguistics & Cognitive Science
entry.content:
I have long been preoccupied with the relationship between linguistics and cognitive science, a tension that has shaped my research identity, my reflections on disciplinary boundaries, and my understanding of what constitutes meaningful, enduring inquiry. What began as technical curiosity has evolved into a sustained philosophical inquiry into the nature of explanation, the politics of academic value, and the fragile bridge between specialized theoretical depth and broad interdisciplinary impact.

My perspective crystallized during a research group meeting in 2025, when I presented a study (not my own) linking syntactic movement to neural activation in Broca’s area. I chose the paper precisely because it integrated formal syntactic theory with neuroscientific evidence, a combination I still consider valuable. After my presentation, a senior collaborator with a strong background in psychology and neuroscience challenged the broader contribution: was the study merely mapping linguistic structures onto brain regions, or did it uncover general principles of cognition? She drew a sharp line between linguistically oriented and psychologically oriented research, arguing that high‑impact journals prioritize questions that resonate across disciplines, not just within a narrow theoretical community. She noted that work confined to linguistic mechanisms often struggles for visibility, funding, and high citation metrics, whereas research framed around general cognitive architecture, like memory, attention, and inhibitory control, attracts wider attention and resources. I pushed back gently, defending the intrinsic value of domain‑specific inquiry, the legitimacy of curiosity‑driven research, and the danger of reducing quality to journal prestige or impact factor. Yet her words stayed with me, forcing me to confront a deeper tension: between the integrity of linguistic theory and the pressure to reframe linguistic questions as windows onto general cognition.

The linguistics stance & the psychology stance
Over time, I have come to see this tension as a defining feature of my intellectual identity. I now distinguish two orientations that often overlap but remain logically distinct: the linguistic stance, which uses experimental methods to understand linguistic structure and its associated mental representation; and the psychological stance, which uses language as a tool to understand general cognitive architecture. The linguistic stance asks: how does the mind compute language? It treats language as a privileged window into uniquely human computational capacities, with its own internal logic, constraints, and developmental timing. The psychological stance asks: how does language reveal general cognition? It treats language as one manifestation of broader systems. In practice, many of my projects embody the first orientation: I begin with a theoretically significant linguistic phenomenon, such as telicity, pronoun resolution, counterfactual conditionals, genitive relative construction, and pseudo‑passive morphology, followed by designing experiments to test how these structures are processed and acquired. My goal is not to reduce language to non‑linguistic functions, but to show how linguistic representations interact with cognitive systems without being exhausted by them.

This positioning has shaped my experience with academic publishing and peer review, revealing deep disciplinary biases in how “importance” is judged. Manuscripts rooted in theoretical linguistics are often criticized in psychology journals as too specialized, too technical, or insufficiently focused on general mechanisms. Reviewers and editors frequently ask me to downplay linguistic theory, prioritize broader cognitive conclusions, and frame effects as instances of more general principles such as similarity‑based interference. I understand this expectation: cognitive science as a field has organized itself around a set of shared problems that cut across domains, and work that can’t be translated into this shared language faces barriers to dissemination. Yet I also resist the implication that linguistically deep research is merely narrow or niche. Linguistics addresses uniquely human questions: how do we compose infinite meanings from finite elements? How do children acquire abstract structural knowledge from limited input? How do crosslinguistic patterns reflect both biological constraints and historical contingency? These are not trivial puzzles; they are foundational to what it means to be human.

My reflections have expanded beyond individual projects to the political economy of knowledge: why some disciplines attract more funding, attention, and prestige than others, even when their intellectual rigor and intrinsic interest are comparable. I have discussed this with peer researchers, asking why theoretical mathematics enjoys stable support while theoretical linguistics struggles for resources, why psychology and neuroscience dominate the cognitive science landscape, and why work framed as “about the brain” often carries more weight than work framed as “about language”. The answer, I have concluded, is not purely scientific but instrumental and narrative. Disciplines thrive when they can tell a compelling story about their social value: mathematics supports national security, technology, and finance; physics promises cosmic insight; neuroscience connects to health, education, and AI. Linguistics, especially formal theoretical linguistics, has struggled to articulate a similarly compelling public narrative. Its contributions are real but often long‑term, indirect, and abstract. Applications such as language teaching, translation technology, or computational linguistics are visible, but they are often disconnected from the core theoretical questions that drive my work. As a result, linguistics remains peripherally positioned within cognitive science, even though language is arguably the most distinctive expression of human cognition.

A commitment, not a compromise
My commitment to a linguistically grounded cognitive science has only strengthened. I reject any choice between linguistic integrity and interdisciplinary impact, instead practicing experimental linguistics that is theoretically responsible, methodologically rigorous, and philosophically reflective. My view of linguistics and cognitive science is integrative, not reductive: language is a privileged part of cognition, revealing unique computational capacities. The mind contains specialized systems that interact dynamically, and my goal is to understand both the specializations and the interactions regarding how linguistic computation operates, develops, varies crosslinguistically, and engages neural systems. I refuse to frame every conclusion as an instance of a broader cognitive principle, just as I refuse to believe that interdisciplinary relevance demands abandoning theoretical depth. Enduring contributions come from those who know their home discipline deeply while speaking across boundaries with clarity. For me, that means remaining a theoretically committed experimental linguist who sharpens linguistic questions rather than diluting them. Language is not just a tool for communication; it is a royal road to the human mind.

entry.title: My Journey Into Linguistics
entry.content:
My academic journey has been shaped by a persistent desire to explore the universal principles and parametric variations underlying natural languages, a shift that began when I transferred from education to linguistics during my undergraduate studies. While education studies offered valuable insights into how policies, values, and practices vary across contexts, I found myself drawn to the pursuit of systematic, universal laws, especially those governing human language.

A pivotal moment in my passion for going deeper into linguistics occurred during an informal discussion with a tutor in my previous B.A. course on Translation: Practice & Theory (Linguistics). After my presentation, he remarked: “Jakobson and Halliday’s research on structural linguistics demonstrates their identity as 70% linguist and 30% semiotician.” This comment reframed my perspective, highlighting how even scholars renowned for their linguistic contributions were not necessarily the representatives of different linguistic schools but extended their inquiries into interdisciplinary realms. The interesting chat prompted me to view interdisciplinarity not as a divergence from linguistics but as a means to enrich and expand the field scope. Inspired by this revelation, I began seeking ways to integrate linguistics with neighboring disciplines.

At The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), I entered M.A. in Applied Linguistics, but I quickly found myself unsettled by how the field often defined “application”, as if application meant leaving the linguistic core behind and attaching oneself to pedagogy, clinical settings, or policy. That never sat right with me. To me, genuine application must ontologically grow from linguistics, not depart from it.

What the public record of my publications does not show is the quiet, humiliating arc of four failed PhD application cycles, each one an education in how the world actually works. The first cycle, 2022-2023, was barely serious: fresh into my M.A., I threw applications to CUHK PhD linguistics and applied linguistics programs, knowing even then I had bare chance. I was testing waters, not crossing them. The second cycle, 2023-2024, was different: I had one SSCI publication, but my research identity was still a fog. I applied only to elite programs, yet I could not have told my clear line of research inquiry. No committee could possibly have extracted coherence from my scattered interests. The rejections were deserved, if painful.

The third cycle, 2024-2025, was when things changed. I had genuine strength: multiple publications, experimental competence, a mature sense of what questions drove me. However, Trump took office, and the funding was cut down. PhD slots shrank mid-cycle. I received waitlists at Ohio State University and Connecticut University, and then rejections. I was finally ready, but the door was narrowing.

The fourth cycle, just past, was my strongest by every metric. My thinking had crystallized; I could defend why my range (from L1 to L2, from children to adults, from behavioral to neuro methods) was not chaotic but coherent around the s-side (syntax/semantics/pragmatics) stance. The published record speaks for itself. Yet the number of funded linguistics PhD slots in America fell even further. I made the waitlist at Northwestern University and UC Santa Cruz. Both ended in no. I learnt from an intended supervisor that I was extremely controversial as my interests are too broad for a department that now needs exceptional fit. Many faculty members even look for specific linguistic phenomenon to supervise. The Stanford student who took the slot even didn't have any offer elsewhere. That is the climate now.

After four cycles, I have learned that admissions is not a meritocracy of ideas. It is a brutal matching game played with shrinking chips, where institutional pedigree, recommendation letter rhetoric, and political funding shifts matter as much as intellectual depth. I am still here, not because I am stubborn, though I am, but because many linguistically-oriented questions remain yet to be answered.
